text: The Same Screen, Three Different People

text: A teacher opens Classeh to assign homework and check who's falling behind. A student opens it to do that homework, and maybe sneak in a game. A parent opens it just to know: is my kid okay?

A teacher opens Classeh to assign homework and check who's falling behind.
A student opens it to do that homework, and maybe sneak in a game.
A parent opens it just to know: is my kid okay?

text: Three completely different reasons to log in. One identical dashboard greeted all of them — a flat grid of look-alike tiles, nothing prioritized, nothing personal. Whatever you actually came for, you had to go hunting for it.
html: Three completely different reasons to log in. One identical dashboard greeted all of them — a flat grid of look-alike tiles, nothing prioritized, nothing personal. Whatever you actually came for, you had to go hunting for it.

text: That grid is where this story starts.

text: Everyone had to dig through everything, just to find the one thing that mattered to them.

text: The old dashboard — the same cluttered grid for every role, with icons that were hard to tell apart at a glance.

text: Here's the catch: I didn't have direct access to students, teachers, or parents. No interviews, no surveys, no seat next to them while they worked. So I started with the only honest thing I could: my own assumptions, based on months of living inside this product:

text: Then I found a better proxy than any dataset: the head of the support team. She hears user frustration every single day, secondhand from the people I couldn't reach directly. I sat down with her, walked through my assumptions one by one, and let her tell me where I was right, and where I wasn't.

text: Sketching the Shape of Three Dashboards

text: With 17+ existing modules and three very different sets of priorities, the question wasn't what to build, it was how to group it so each role saw their world, not everyone else's.
html: With 17+ existing modules and three very different sets of priorities, the question wasn't what to build, it was how to group it so each role saw their world, not everyone else's.

text: Working module by module with the support lead, I sorted tiles by what people were actually trying to accomplish, not by how the system happened to file them internally.

text: My first real attempt at solving this was a sidebar, a rough version, shared early instead of perfected alone. The CTO shut it down instantly:
html:
My first real attempt at solving this was a sidebar, a rough version, shared early instead of perfected alone.
The CTO shut it down instantly:

text: | "I know this sidebar model is outdated and won't work for us."
html: |  "I know this sidebar model is outdated and won't work for us."

text: No explanation followed. And, in the moment, I didn't ask for one. But not everything in it was wrong. The shortcuts inside the sidebar were approved, so I kept them and just changed where they lived.

text: First, the icons. I reworked every tile icon with distinct colors and simple, memorable shapes, so a module could be recognized at a glance, no label required.
html: First, the icons. I reworked every tile icon with distinct colors and simple, memorable shapes, so a module could be recognized at a glance, no label required.

text: Reworked icons — playful, colorful shapes for the student side, a more restrained style for teachers and parents — all designed with distinct colors and simple, memorable shapes so users can recognize a module at a glance.
html: Reworked icons — playful, colorful shapes for the student side, a more restrained style for teachers and parents — all designed with distinct colors and simple, memorable shapes so users can recognize a module at a glance.

text: The old icons — similar colors and busy shapes made it hard to tell modules apart without reading the label.
html: The old icons — similar colors and busy shapes made it hard to tell modules apart without reading the label.

text: Then, the structure. I took the sidebar's categorization logic, the one part that had survived, and brought it straight into the dashboard, now renamed the Hub. Modules were grouped by purpose instead of scattered as identical tiles, with each role's top priority surfaced first.
html: Then, the structure. I took the sidebar's categorization logic, the one part that had survived, and brought it straight into the dashboard, now renamed the Hub. Modules were grouped by purpose instead of scattered as identical tiles, with each role's top priority surfaced first.

text: The Hub — modules grouped by purpose instead of scattered as identical tiles, using the same categorization logic from the rejected sidebar.
html: The Hub — modules grouped by purpose instead of scattered as identical tiles, using the same categorization logic from the rejected sidebar.

text: As a teacher, I want to assign something to my students then check if they’re doing it right.
html: As a teacher, I want to assign something to my students then check if they’re doing it right.

text: As a student, I want to do a task assigned to me, such as doing a homework.

text: I handed off fully organized, labeled screens in Figma, then sat with our frontend developer for the final stretch, checking components and styles against the live code, screen by screen, until what shipped matched what was designed.
html: I handed off fully organized, labeled screens in Figma, then sat with our frontend developer for the final stretch, checking components and styles against the live code, screen by screen, until what shipped matched what was designed.

text: The redesigned Hub drove close to a 10% improvement in dashboard performance, tracked through Microsoft Clarity.
html: The redesigned Hub drove close to a 10% improvement in dashboard performance, tracked through Microsoft Clarity.

text: But the number I care about more is this: the same support channel that used to collect complaints started collecting thank-you calls instead.
html: But the number I care about more is this: the same support channel that used to collect complaints started collecting thank-you calls instead.

text: Three roles, one platform, each one now opening on exactly what they came to do.
html: Three roles, one platform, each one now opening on exactly what they came to do.

text: A rejection without a reason leaves a question open, even when you agree with it.
html: A rejection without a reason leaves a question open, even when you agree with it.

text: I wasn't unhappy with the outcome. I had my own doubts about the sidebar before the CTO said anything, and his rejection matched what I already felt. But to this day, I don't know if it was actually wrong, or just not our taste. He never said, and I never asked.
html: I wasn't unhappy with the outcome. I had my own doubts about the sidebar before the CTO said anything, and his rejection matched what I already felt. But to this day, I don't know if it was actually wrong, or just not our taste. He never said, and I never asked.

text: Since then, I've learned to close that gap before moving on, even when I already agree with the call. Asking why isn't about doubting the outcome, it's about not carrying an unresolved question into the next decision.
html: Since then, I've learned to close that gap before moving on, even when I already agree with the call. Asking why isn't about doubting the outcome, it's about not carrying an unresolved question into the next decision.

text: My next step in learning is figuring out how to get the answer to that question without creating tension or bad feelings. Hard human skills! :)
